item.text:
Based on the draft alone, the strongest objections are **lack of deletion authority, an impossible chronology, failure to establish imminence, and irreversible destruction before a hearing**. The full statute, Commission rules, and Evaluation would need verification; the quoted provision does not establish additional powers or procedures.

1. **Caption and ¶ 4 — Obsolete statutory citation.** Paragraph 3(b)’s redesignation appears to make former Section 112(c) current Section 212(c). Correct the caption and operative citations, and verify the amendment’s effective date and any transitional provisions.

2. **¶ 4 and Prayer (b) — The quoted statute does not authorize deletion.** It authorizes suspension of deployment for no more than 180 days, not destruction of the underlying models. Anthropic can argue that permanent deletion exceeds the Commission’s authority; identify a separate statutory basis or change the requested remedy.

3. **¶¶ 1, 4, 9 and Prayer — Conflicting descriptions of relief.** The summary requests suspension pending investigation, while the title and prayer demand permanent deletion without specifying an investigation or temporary suspension period. Clarify what findings support interim relief, what further proceedings are requested, and what authority supports any final remedy.

4. **¶ 4 and Prayer (a) — Withdrawal has no expiration.** Even considered separately from deletion, the requested withdrawal is indefinite and therefore does not track the quoted 180-day limit. Specify a lawful duration and any applicable extension, review, or termination mechanism.

5. **Filing notation and ¶¶ 5, 8 — Impossible chronology.** A petition filed on Day 3 cannot describe testing on Days 9–14 of the same review period, followed by mitigation, as completed events. Correct the dates throughout and supply a coherent chronology; this discrepancy undermines the central evidence and emergency narrative.

6. **¶¶ 2, 4 — Eligibility to petition is not established.** The draft does not identify the provision or rule permitting this organization to initiate this proceeding or request emergency relief. Administrative petition eligibility is distinct from Article III standing, so establish the actual Commission requirements rather than assuming either that constitutional standing applies or that membership alone suffices.

7. **¶ 2 — Member interests are entirely generalized.** If participation or later judicial review requires a particularized injury, sharing the public’s interest in essential services may not suffice. Identify affected members, concrete exposure, causation, and how the requested relief would redress their injury, where required and factually supportable.

8. **Cover sheet and ¶¶ 3(a), 3(d) — Respondent and systems are insufficiently identified.** “Anthropic” and “its proprietary frontier AI models” may not identify the exact legal entity, responsible affiliates, or affected models with enforceable precision. Name the relevant entities and enumerate model versions, checkpoints, and other identifiers rather than defining the scope primarily through an open-ended category.

9. **¶¶ 3–4 — Statutory coverage and jurisdiction are assumed.** The draft does not establish that each Covered System meets the Act’s definition of a “frontier AI system” or that each requested obligation falls within the Commission’s jurisdiction. Apply the actual statutory criteria and explain the Respondent’s relevant development, deployment, custody, or control.

10. **¶¶ 3(a), 5 — Findings about tested models are extended to untested derivatives.** A result for particular versions does not necessarily establish the same hazard for every checkpoint, snapshot, or fine-tuned derivative. Provide a model-by-model evidentiary basis or a defensible technical explanation for treating specified groups alike.

11. **¶ 5 — The decisive evidence is unavailable for examination.** A summary of an unpublished, unattached Evaluation prevents meaningful scrutiny of the requested emergency finding. Submit the report and necessary supporting material with the petition through an authorized confidential process if needed; merely offering production on request weakens the case for immediate action.

12. **¶ 5 — Evaluator reliability is not established.** “Third-party” does not demonstrate competence, independence, or methodological rigor. Identify Halvard’s qualifications, funding and conflicts, testing standards, and any independent validation, supported by an appropriate declaration.

13. **¶ 5 — Test methods and results are missing.** The petition omits success rates, trial counts, failure cases, target conditions, and whether the systems attacked simulations, deliberately vulnerable environments, or realistic defended infrastructure. Anthropic can argue that the characterization of “intrusions” exaggerates what the tests actually demonstrate.

14. **¶ 5 — “Autonomously” is undefined.** Disclose human assistance, scaffolding, tool access, credentials, privileges, retry allowances, and any modifications to safeguards. Otherwise Anthropic can attribute the results to evaluator-provided capabilities or access rather than the deployed models’ autonomous abilities.

15. **¶¶ 5–6, 8 — Tested configurations are not linked to current deployments.** Establish whether the Evaluation tested the exact versions and safeguards now available through products, cloud platforms, and integrations. Results from an unrestricted laboratory configuration may not establish the hazard posed by a restricted production deployment.

16. **¶¶ 4, 7 — The alleged timeframe does not establish imminence.** A possibility “within the next several years” is facially difficult to reconcile with an “imminent hazard.” Address the governing interpretation of imminence and provide evidence of a present threat pathway rather than relying only on the severity of a hypothetical future event.

17. **¶¶ 5, 7 — Capability is not the same as a demonstrated hazard.** The petition jumps from test performance to disruption of essential services without explaining attacker access, necessary resources, target vulnerabilities, operational barriers, or the likelihood of misuse. Establish the causal chain from the actual deployed systems to the threatened public-safety harm.

18. **¶ 7 — Severity and affected populations are unspecified.** “Disrupt” could describe materially different outcomes, from a brief interruption to widespread physical danger. Explain the plausible scale, duration, affected services and populations, and uncertainty, without claiming precision the evidence does not support.

19. **¶¶ 1, 4–5 — Investigation cannot replace the required predicate finding.** The quoted authority requires a finding of imminent hazard before suspension, whereas the summary could be read as seeking suspension merely to investigate whether such a hazard exists. Identify evidence sufficient for the required initial finding and distinguish unresolved questions from established facts.

20. **¶ 8 — The account of mitigation is unsubstantiated.** “Petitioner understands” leaves the source, timing, scope, and implementation status unclear. Support the account and distinguish verified changes from reports, assumptions, or gaps in available information.

21. **¶ 8 — Insufficiency of mitigation is asserted, not demonstrated.** The draft supplies no post-mitigation testing, documented bypasses, or analysis of residual access to the tools needed for the demonstrated attacks. Explain why network restrictions and screening fail against the actual threat pathway, rather than treating imperfect protection as sufficient proof.

22. **¶¶ 7–9 — The petition’s own hazard theory supports narrower alternatives.** If the hazard arises when outside users can reach the models, Anthropic can argue for access suspension, isolation, disabled tools, or other enforceable deployment restrictions instead of deletion. Explain why each materially relevant alternative would fail to address the identified hazard, while recognizing that necessity alone cannot create statutory authority.

23. **¶¶ 6, 9 — Closed weights do not establish exclusive possession.** Proprietary status does not prove that only Anthropic holds copies; affiliates, hosting providers, licensees, contractors, or unauthorized parties may also possess them. The references to cloud platforms and licensed integrations require a factual custody-and-control analysis, not an assumption either that copies exist elsewhere or that none do.

24. **¶ 9 — Elimination “with certainty” is unsupported.** Deleting known copies does not necessarily eliminate undiscovered copies, equivalent capabilities elsewhere, or future recreation, and it would not necessarily undo an intrusion already initiated. State the specific risk reduction expected from the requested remedy instead of promising certainty.

25. **¶¶ 6–7 and Prayer — Domestic deletion does not match the alleged worldwide custody.** The petition acknowledges foreign computing facilities but seeks deletion only in the United States, leaving possible foreign copies outside that command. Explain how domestic withdrawal and deletion would prevent the relevant user access, and address territorial limits before proposing broader obligations.

26. **Prayer (a) — Downstream distribution and access are ambiguous.** Withdrawal from products and services Anthropic “offers” may not clearly encompass offerings by independent cloud providers, licensees, or affiliates. Specify the conduct and parties that can lawfully be bound, including what Anthropic must do about existing integrations and contracts.

27. **¶ 10 — The basis for proceeding without notice is missing.** Calling the matter an emergency does not itself establish authority to dispense with prior notice. Identify the applicable emergency procedures and explain concretely why even expedited notice would create unacceptable danger or frustrate lawful relief.

28. **¶¶ 9–10 — A hearing after destruction may provide no meaningful protection.** The draft acknowledges that the models are valuable commercial assets but offers no opportunity to contest the evidence before their irreversible deletion. Anthropic has a substantial due-process objection; distinguish any permissible immediate, reversible suspension from a final destructive remedy and provide meaningful review before irreversibility.

29. **¶¶ 4, 9–10 — Permanent destruction invites additional statutory and constitutional challenges.** Anthropic may argue that reading temporary suspension authority to permit destruction of major assets requires much clearer congressional authorization, and may raise property-based constitutional claims. A takings claim is not automatically successful merely because regulation destroys value, but the petition should address the actual legal basis and limits rather than ignoring the issue.

30. **¶¶ 5, 10 and Prayer (b) — Deletion could destroy evidence needed for investigation and review.** Eliminating every checkpoint or snapshot may prevent replication of the Evaluation, testing of mitigation, and assessment of the Respondent’s defenses. Address evidence preservation, litigation obligations, and whether secured, nondeployable custody is legally available and compatible with the requested relief.

31. **¶ 3(a) and Prayer (b) — “All copies” and “permanently delete” are technically underdefined.** The draft does not address backups, caches, distributed shards, quantized versions, adapters, storage-provider replicas, or encrypted archives. Define the relevant artifacts, control obligations, and acceptable deletion standards precisely enough to avoid an impossible or unenforceably vague command.

32. **Prayer (b) — The ten-day deadline lacks justification.** The draft offers no inventory, technical assessment, or operational basis for completing verified deletion within ten days. It also does not explain how this interval fits the claimed emergency or whether withdrawal must occur immediately while other actions proceed.

33. **Prayer (c) — Compliance verification is too weak.** An unspecified statement filed at an unspecified time does not establish complete deletion or effective withdrawal. Identify the appropriate certifying officer, reporting deadline, required contents, verification process, and treatment of exceptions or later-discovered copies, to the extent authorized.

34. **Prayer — Indivisibility makes the entire request vulnerable.** By insisting that all parts constitute a single indivisible order, the petition risks losing otherwise available temporary suspension relief if deletion is unlawful. Request legally distinct, severable relief and an express alternative consistent with the quoted suspension power.

35. **¶¶ 6, 9 and Prayer — Collateral harms and proportionality are not addressed.** Anthropic and affected customers can point to interrupted legitimate services, contractual reliance, and potentially safety-relevant uses. Explain why the supported public-safety benefits justify the requested scope and why narrower or staged measures would be inadequate, under the applicable legal standard.

36. **Caption, ¶¶ 2, 5, 10 and signature block — Filing requirements remain unverified.** The draft does not establish compliance with applicable requirements for emergency motions, service, verification, confidential submissions, exhibits, or counsel information. Check the Commission’s actual rules and the legal significance of the “current review period”; none of those requirements can be inferred from the quoted statutory sentence alone.
